guides.title: EMA 9 initial seed and smoothing weight
guides.concept: EMA9 uses alpha=2/(9+1)=0.2 and recursively blends the latest completed close with a previously seeded EMA.
guides.procedure: Count nine completed historical closes; seed with their SMA, then apply alpha only at the next completed bar.
guides.workedCase: FICTIONAL: Nine closes have arithmetic mean $10.00; the tenth completed close is $10.50. EMA9 becomes 0.2×10.50+0.8×10.00=$10.10.
guides.limit: Early calculations depend on seed and prehistory; EMA9 cannot verify the following candle.

guides.commonError: Calculating an EMA9 on fewer than nine completed closes under an SMA seed convention.

guides.title: EMA 200 availability after a full observation window
guides.concept: An SMA-seeded EMA200 needs at least 200 valid completed closes for an initialized number, not 199 provisional values.
guides.procedure: Count completed observations; construct the first SMA seed from exactly 200 closes, then apply alpha=2/201 to later closes.
guides.workedCase: FICTIONAL: 199 completed closes mean EMA200 is unavailable. With 200 completed closes all at $20, seed=$20; a 201st close at $21 creates EMA200≈$20.00995.
guides.limit: A flat synthetic price history does not substitute for real price feeds or 200-day evidence; vendor histories can differ.
guides.invalidation: Do not calculate or interpret this explanation if required sourced data, timestamps, units or the declared observation window are unavailable. A flat synthetic price history does not substitute for real price feeds or 200-day evidence; vendor histories can differ.

guides.title: True range includes the previous close when prices gap
guides.concept: True range is max(high−low, |high−previous close|, |low−previous close|) for completed OHLC bars.
guides.procedure: Compare three distances using the prior completed close, current completed high and current completed low.
guides.workedCase: FICTIONAL: Previous close $10, next high $10.80, low $10.60: distances $0.20, $0.80 and $0.60; true range is $0.80.
guides.limit: One true-range observation is not a smoothed Average True Range; no previous close means a missing gap reference.
guides.invalidation: Do not calculate or interpret this explanation if required sourced data, timestamps, units or the declared observation window are unavailable. One true-range observation is not a smoothed Average True Range; no previous close means a missing gap reference.

guides.title: Population versus sample standard deviation denominators
guides.concept: A sample standard deviation uses n−1 for n>1; a population standard deviation uses n. The choice affects the answer.
guides.procedure: Calculate the average of returns, square each deviation, divide by the explicitly chosen denominator, and take the square root.
guides.workedCase: FICTIONAL: Returns +1%, 0%, −1% have mean 0; population SD≈0.8165 percentage points; sample SD=1 percentage point.
guides.limit: A historical sample does not establish the distribution of future returns or make volatile assets forecastable.
guides.invalidation: Do not calculate or interpret this explanation if required sourced data, timestamps, units or the declared observation window are unavailable. A historical sample does not establish the distribution of future returns or make volatile assets forecastable.
guides.commonError: Describing a calculation divided by n as if it were a sample estimate divided by n−1.

guides.concept: Under an expressly stated scaling convention, annualized volatility approximates daily standard deviation × sqrt(annual sessions).

guides.title: Price change in dollars versus simple percentage return
guides.concept: An absolute dollar price move and a simple percentage return answer different questions; the denominator is the initial price.
guides.procedure: Compute later price minus earlier price and then divide by earlier price to express the move as a percentage.
guides.workedCase: FICTIONAL: $10 to $11 is +$1/share or +10%; $50 to $51 is also +$1/share but only +2%.
guides.limit: Dividends and split adjustments may change economic total return relative to a raw price chart.

guides.title: Drawdown measured from the maximum observed so far
guides.concept: A drawdown compares current value to the highest prior or current observed value, never a future high that was unknown at the time.
guides.procedure: At each past timestamp update only the running maximum; drawdown=current/running peak−1.
guides.workedCase: FICTIONAL: Portfolio index peaks at 100, drops to 90, then rises to 96. Drawdowns are −10% and −4% respectively.
guides.limit: Drawdown is a historical path measure, not a certainty that the next price will fall or recover.
guides.invalidation: Do not calculate or interpret this explanation if required sourced data, timestamps, units or the declared observation window are unavailable. Drawdown is a historical path measure, not a certainty that the next price will fall or recover.

guides.concept: A two-outcome expected P/L multiplies each conditional payoff by its assumed probability and sums both terms.

guides.title: Break-even win percentage including a fixed transaction cost
guides.concept: For hypothetical constant gross win W, loss L and cost C per attempt, break-even p=(L+C)/(W+L).
guides.procedure: Solve pW−(1−p)L−C=0 after assigning positive payoff W, positive loss magnitude L and cost units.
guides.workedCase: FICTIONAL: Gross win $20, loss $10 and average cost $2 give (10+2)/(20+10)=40% break-even win rate.
guides.limit: A fixed win/loss approximation can miss fat tails, variable costs and slippage; it does not estimate the actual p.
guides.invalidation: Do not calculate or interpret this explanation if required sourced data, timestamps, units or the declared observation window are unavailable. A fixed win/loss approximation can miss fat tails, variable costs and slippage; it does not estimate the actual p.

guides.concept: A listed equity-option premium is commonly quoted per underlying share, while a standard equity contract generally covers 100 shares.

guides.title: Call option intrinsic value versus extrinsic premium
guides.concept: A call's current intrinsic value equals max(stock price−strike,0); positive option premium above intrinsic represents extrinsic value.
guides.procedure: Match the underlying and option quote timestamps and subtract nonnegative intrinsic value from the option premium.
guides.workedCase: FICTIONAL: A call with strike $50, underlying $55 and per-share premium $7 has $5 intrinsic and $2 extrinsic value.
guides.limit: Quoted option values vary with volatility, time and market prices; this does not guarantee a liquid exit.
guides.invalidation: Do not calculate or interpret this explanation if required sourced data, timestamps, units or the declared observation window are unavailable. Quoted option values vary with volatility, time and market prices; this does not guarantee a liquid exit.

guides.title: Long call break-even at expiration is strike plus premium
guides.concept: At option expiration, a long call's intrinsic payout must cover its original per-share premium for a break-even before fees.
guides.procedure: Calculate expiration intrinsic=max(stock−strike,0); net premium-adjusted payoff=intrinsic−original premium.
guides.workedCase: FICTIONAL: Long call strike $50 and original premium $2.20 has expiration break-even $52.20; stock $51 at expiration still implies a loss.
guides.limit: This is an expiration payoff, not a required price for positive interim resale or an actionable forecast.

guides.concept: Operating cash-flow margin compares cash from operations with same-period revenue; it is not net income margin or free cash flow.
guides.procedure: Get both operating cash flow and revenue for the same issuer and comparable period, then divide CFO by revenue.
guides.workedCase: FICTIONAL: Operating cash flow $15 million and annual revenue $100 million imply CFO margin 15%. Capital expenditure is not subtracted yet.
guides.limit: Cash collection timing and working capital shifts matter, so one period's high CFO margin is not a durable forecast.
